items.stem: Why can the same molecule be written as several different valid SMILES strings?

options.text: SMILES depends on the chosen starting atom and traversal order, so canonicalisation is needed
options.rationale: Correct: canonical SMILES gives one standard string per molecule.

options.text: SMILES strings are always unique for each molecule
Because the molecule changes structure each time
options.rationale: The structure is unchanged; only the string representation differs.

items.stem: Which TWO steps help prevent data leakage in a cheminformatics model? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Splitting train and test sets by molecular scaffold
options.rationale: Correct: scaffold splits keep near-duplicates out of both sets.
Correct: duplicates across splits leak information.

options.text: Tuning hyperparameters on the test set
options.rationale: That leaks test information into training.

options.text: Random splitting of highly similar analogues
options.rationale: Random splits let near-duplicates cross the boundary.

items.explanation: Correct: scaffold splits keep near-duplicates out of both sets.

items.stem: What does a Tanimoto coefficient of 0.9 between two fingerprints indicate?

options.text: The molecules are highly similar by that fingerprint, though not necessarily identical
options.rationale: Correct: high similarity is not proof of the same structure.

options.text: The molecules are definitely the same compound
options.rationale: High similarity does not guarantee identity.
A high value indicates many shared features.

options.text: The value is invalid because it exceeds 0.5
options.rationale: Tanimoto values range from 0 to 1; 0.9 is valid.

items.explanation: Correct: high similarity is not proof of the same structure.
